chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Momentum and Trend Following Actually Are

lessons.title: Trend Following vs Momentum: Two Related but Distinct Ideas

children.text: On the same morning in Mumbai, two traders place very different bets. The first, running a systematic commodity book, goes long MCX gold futures because gold has been trading above its rising 200-day moving average for weeks, an uptrend by his definition, regardless of what any other commodity or stock is doing. The second, running an equity screen on Nifty 200 stocks, buys the fifteen stocks that have outperformed the other 185 over the past six months, some of which are barely up in absolute terms but have still beaten their peers. Both traders would probably describe themselves as following momentum. Only one of them, strictly speaking, is.

body.text: Trend following asks a single question about one asset at a time: is this asset trending up or down, judged against its own history? Momentum, in its classic academic sense, asks a comparative question across many assets: is this asset outperforming its peers? The two ideas are closely related and often used interchangeably in casual conversation, but they are built differently and behave differently.

children.text: Trend Following: An Absolute Bet on One Asset's Direction

markDefs.definition: A strategy that judges a single asset against its own price history to determine whether it is trending up or down, with no comparison to other assets. Also called time-series momentum.

children.text: looks at a single asset in isolation and asks only whether its own price is trending up or down relative to its own recent history. It makes no comparison to any other asset. Gold does not need to be beating crude oil for a trend follower to go long gold. Nifty futures do not need to be beating the Sensex for a trend follower to go long the index. All that matters is the asset's own trend, typically measured with tools like moving averages, covered in full in Chapter 2. Because it evaluates each asset independently, trend following can and does go short assets in a downtrend, not just long assets in an uptrend, and it applies equally to equities, commodities, currencies, and bonds. This is the approach used by global managed futures funds, often called CTAs, commodity trading advisors, which trade trend signals across dozens of futures markets at the same time.
Momentum: A Relative Bet Across Many Assets

markDefs.definition: A momentum strategy built by ranking a universe of comparable securities against each other by recent return, rather than judging any one of them in isolation.

children.text: Momentum, in the sense introduced in Lesson 1 and formalized by Jegadeesh and Titman, works differently. It starts with a universe of comparable securities, say all Nifty 200 stocks, ranks them against each other by recent return, and buys the top performers while typically avoiding or shorting the bottom performers. This is a relative, or

, comparison: a stock can be included in a momentum portfolio even if its own absolute return is mediocre, as long as it has outperformed most of its peers in the same universe. This cross-sectional framing, and how it differs formally from the time-series framing used in trend following, is covered in depth in Chapter 4.

body.text: In casual market conversation, 'momentum' and 'trend following' are often used as if they mean the same thing. In this course they don't. Trend following is single-asset and absolute. Momentum, unless specified otherwise, means cross-sectional and relative. Keep this distinction in mind for the rest of the course, it affects how each strategy is built, tested, and risk-managed.

columns.label: Trend Following
points: Evaluates one asset against its own price history
Can go long or short depending on the trend's direction
Applies across equities, commodities, currencies, and bonds
Typically built on moving averages or similar filters
Also called time-series momentum in academic literature

columns.label: Momentum
points: Ranks a universe of assets against each other
Typically long the top ranked, avoids or shorts the bottom ranked
Most commonly applied within a single asset class, usually equities
Typically built on trailing return ranking
Formally called cross-sectional momentum in academic literature

children.text: A Real Example: NSE's Own Momentum Index

You don't have to build a momentum strategy from scratch to see one in action. NSE Indices, the index arm of the NSE, publishes the Nifty200 Momentum 30 Index, built directly on cross-sectional momentum logic. It starts with the Nifty 200 universe, scores each stock using a combination of its 6-month and 12-month price return adjusted for volatility, and holds the 30 highest-scoring stocks, rebalanced periodically. It is a live, public, rules-based example of exactly the ranking process introduced in Lesson 1, running on real Indian large and mid-cap stocks. Check the current methodology document on niftyindices.com before assuming any detail here still applies, index methodologies are reviewed and can change over time.

body.value: A published, rules-based cross-sectional momentum index
body.context: Ranks the Nifty 200 universe by volatility-adjusted 6-month and 12-month return, and holds the top 30. A real example of cross-sectional momentum, not the trend-following approach covered next.

children.text: A Real Example: Trend Following Beyond Equities

Trend following's natural habitat is not equities alone, it is any market with a liquid futures contract. On MCX, a trend follower can go long or short gold, silver, or crude oil purely based on each contract's own price trend, with no need to compare it to any other commodity. Globally, this is a large, established institutional strategy: managed futures funds and CTAs collectively run a substantial pool of capital applying trend rules, mostly moving-average and breakout based, across currencies, bonds, equity indices, and commodities at the same time. In India, retail access to pure multi-asset trend following is more limited than in equities, but the same logic is used by traders running systematic strategies on Nifty and Bank Nifty futures through a broker's API, for example Zerodha's Kite Connect, subject to SEBI's algorithmic trading framework.

body.title: Trend following or momentum?
body.question: A trader buys Bank Nifty futures because the index has been making higher highs and higher lows above its rising 50-day moving average, with no reference to how any other index or asset is performing. Which is this?
options: Cross-sectional momentum, because it compares the index to its peers
Trend following, because it is an absolute judgement on one asset's own price direction
Value investing, because moving averages are a valuation tool
Arbitrage, because two prices are involved
body.explanation: There is no peer comparison here at all, only a judgement about Bank Nifty's own price relative to its own moving average. That is the defining feature of trend following, also called time-series momentum.

body.title: Complete the definition
body.textWithBlank: Trend following is an absolute bet on one asset's own direction, while momentum, unless specified otherwise, refers to a ___ bet across many assets.
body.explanation: Momentum, in its classic academic sense, ranks a universe of assets against each other rather than judging any single one in isolation. That relative, or cross-sectional, comparison is what separates it from trend following.

body.title: Classify the strategy
body.scenario: A systematic fund manager builds a strategy that goes long Nifty 50 stocks whose trailing 6-month return ranks in the top quartile of the index, and separately goes long MCX gold because gold's own price is above its rising 200-day moving average.
body.prompt: Which part of this strategy is momentum, and which part is trend following? Why?
body.modelAnswer: The Nifty 50 stock selection is cross-sectional momentum: it ranks stocks against each other within one universe, the index, and picks the top performers by relative return. The gold position is trend following: it is a single-asset, absolute judgement based on gold's own price relative to its own moving average, with no comparison to any other asset. The manager is running both ideas side by side, in two different parts of the same portfolio.

body.title: Trend Following vs Momentum: Core Terms

cards.definition: A strategy that judges a single asset against its own price history to determine whether it is trending up or down, with no comparison to other assets.
The academic term for trend following, an absolute, single-asset judgement based on that asset's own past returns.
The academic term for classic momentum, ranking a universe of assets against each other by recent return and buying the relative top performers.
A fund manager who runs systematic trend-following strategies, typically across many futures markets and asset classes at once.
A strategy's return judged on its own terms, without comparison to a peer group or benchmark, the framing trend following uses.

points: Trend following is a single-asset, absolute judgement on direction: is this asset trending up or down against its own history?
Momentum, in its classic sense, is a cross-sectional, relative judgement: is this asset outperforming its peers within a defined universe?
Trend following can go long or short and applies across equities, commodities, currencies, and bonds, wherever a liquid instrument exists.
Momentum is most commonly applied within a single asset class, usually equities, and is typically long the top-ranked names.
NSE's own Nifty200 Momentum 30 Index is a live, public example of cross-sectional momentum running on real Indian stocks.
The formal academic distinction between time-series and cross-sectional momentum, and the research behind each, is covered in depth in Chapter 4.
